ai_summary: Great Britain is currently generating 6.1 GW of wind power, with estimated Scottish wind output reaching 1.8 GW, representing 17.8% of installed Scottish wind capacity. This clean generation maintains a Scottish carbon intensity of 0 gCO2/kWh, standing in sharp contrast to the broader GB-wide carbon intensity of 194 gCO2/kWh. However, transmission bottlenecks continue to enforce severe constraints across the network. Scottish generation curtailed so far today stands at 578 MWh, turned down through Balancing Mechanism bids at a constraint cost of about £38,647. Because this surplus renewable power cannot reach downstream demand centres, thermal plants must compensate elsewhere, resulting in an estimated 109,801 m3 of gas burned elsewhere to replace it and releasing 202 tonnes of additional CO2. Extrapolating today’s constraint run-rate suggests an estimated total yearly cost of curtailment of £14 million. When socialised across national electricity consumption, this recurring system friction increases everybody's invoice in the UK by an estimated £0.05/MWh, highlighting how grid infrastructure deficits impose both a direct financial levy on consumers and an unnecessary carbon penalty on the energy transition.
